clue.text: Drove spear viciously into coat

indicators.note: something done viciously is done with wild violence, so the letters are thrown about into a new order

blocks.note: the ten letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone drives a spear savagely into an animal's hide or a soldier's coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coat' looks like a garment, but here it is the verb: to spread a layer over something.
explanation.definitionFit: To overspread a surface is to cover it entirely with a layer, which is what coating means.

clue.text: Carry out the old bishop with ring uplifted

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting the letters up makes them read from bottom to top

blocks.note: ye is the archaic form of 'the', as in Ye Olde Shoppe
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
a ring is round like the letter O

explanation.surface: Pallbearers carry out the coffin of an old bishop, his ring raised aloft.
explanation.definitionFit: To obey an order is to carry it out, as instructed, without refusal.

clue.text: Food worries

blocks.note: first meaning: informal plural noun for things to eat
second meaning: as in 'what's eating you?', it troubles or bothers

explanation.walkthrough: The two words read like a phrase about anxiety over meals, but each is a separate meaning of one short word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is slang for food as a plural noun, and as a verb it means gnaws at someone's peace of mind.

clue.text: It is held by the journeyman regularly to reduce costs

definitions.text: It is held by the journeyman regularly to reduce costs

blocks.clueFragment: It is held by the journeyman regularly
blocks.note: surface reading: a skilled tradesman who has served his apprenticeship keeps hold of some tool
setter's reading: a commuter making the same journey every day buys a pass covering many trips at a discount

explanation.walkthrough: 'Journeyman' normally means a qualified craftsman, and 'regularly' looks like a signal to take alternate letters; both are red herrings. Here the journeyman is simply someone who travels.
explanation.definitionFit: A commuter's long-term travel pass is bought up front and works out cheaper per trip than daily fares.

clue.text: Searches vigorously for such authentic music

blocks.note: first meaning: as a pig digs with its snout, rummages about
second meaning: traditional folk or reggae music thought to be close to its origins

explanation.surface: A collector hunts hard through record bins for genuine, unpolished music.
explanation.definitionFit: To root about is to dig and rummage, and roots music is the name for traditional, grass-level folk styles.

clue.text: Uncle Sam's things recollected in a camera

indicators.note: read as re-collected, gathered up again in a different arrangement

blocks.note: the nine letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Souvenirs of a trip to the United States are remembered through holiday snaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recollected' looks like remembering; split it as re-collected and it becomes the signal. Uncle Sam personifies the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: Americana are objects and artefacts characteristic of the United States, the nation Uncle Sam stands for.

clue.text: Without women, theatre closed prematurely

indicators.note: a word closed early stops short, losing its final letter

blocks.note: the stage stands for the theatre as a profession

explanation.surface: A show with an all-male cast shut down before the end of its run.
explanation.definitionFit: A stag party or stag night is a gathering for men only, so the adjective means with no women present.

clue.text: A satire about English flat development

blocks.clueFragment: A satire about English flat development
blocks.note: surface reading: a comic piece mocking how England's blocks of flats get built
setter's reading: the title of Jonathan Swift's 1704 satire on religious excess

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the title of Swift's satire. The clue's tail is a playful gloss on that title rather than a strict letter-by-letter construction.
explanation.definitionFit: Swift's 1704 prose work mocks corruption in religion and learning, and is one of the best-known satires in English.

clue.text: Plucky museum official, who once poached?

definitions.note: the answer is a noun; the definition reads as a description of one

blocks.note: game means brave and willing, as in 'game for anything'
a keeper is a curator in charge of a museum collection

explanation.surface: A brave museum curator turns out to have a past as a poacher.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the saying 'poacher turned gamekeeper': the man guarding the estate's game may once have stolen it.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb holds that the best guardian of an estate's birds was formerly a poacher himself, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Second sweater needed for him?

blocks.note: surface reading: an additional jumper, worn for warmth on a cold day
setter's reading: a fielder at a particular position in cricket, who stands out in the chill

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, extra cover is a fielding position on the off side, between cover and mid-off. Read literally, the name is a second layer of clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Taken word by word, the fielding position's name describes an additional garment, which is what a second sweater is.

clue.text: In downhill race look out for crash

indicators.note: out tells us the following short word is removed from the race's name

blocks.note: a slalom is a ski race weaving down a slope between gates
lo is the old word for look, as in 'lo and behold'

explanation.surface: A warning to ski racers to watch out for a fall on the course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' and 'look out' read as a warning; the race contains the word for look, and taking it away leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A slam is a violent, noisy impact, so it serves as a synonym for a crash.

clue.text: Giving nasty looks? Alice never heard of such a thing!

blocks.note: surface reading: glaring at someone

blocks.clueFragment: Alice never heard of such a thing!
blocks.note: setter's reading: in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, the Mock Turtle's lessons include a made-up subject that baffles Alice

explanation.walkthrough: 'Giving nasty looks' suggests scowling, but it means making something ugly. Lewis Carroll's Mock Turtle studies this mock-arithmetic subject and Alice says she never heard of it.
explanation.definitionFit: The coined noun means the act of making ugly, that is, bestowing an unpleasant appearance.

clue.text: Health-giving device for getting brown

blocks.note: surface reading: a sunlamp or tanning bed, good for you and for your tan
setter's reading: drinking a health is proposing a toast, and the device browns bread over a fire

explanation.walkthrough: 'Health-giving' sounds medical, but to give a health is to raise a glass to someone, so the first word is a pun on the kitchen sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The long-handled utensil holds bread to a fire until it browns, and its first word also means drinking healths.

clue.text: Obstetrician attending bed in one old city

indicators.note: in places the furniture word inside the letters standing for one old city

blocks.note: an ace is the one in a pack of cards
a couch is a bed or sofa
Ur was an ancient Sumerian city in Mesopotamia

explanation.surface: A doctor attends a woman in childbirth at a bedside in an ancient city.
explanation.definitionFit: The French-derived word names a man who assists at births, a male midwife or obstetrician.

clue.text: What the Ancient Mariner did to people in the spray

definitions.text: What the Ancient Mariner did to people
definitions.note: the answer is the verb the description names, not the past tense

blocks.clueFragment: What the Ancient Mariner did to people
blocks.note: first meaning: in Coleridge's poem the Mariner stops a wedding guest and detains him with his tale
second meaning: a small spray of flowers worn on a lapel

explanation.surface: Coleridge's old sailor seized people as the sea spray flew around them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spray' looks like sea foam in a poem about the sea, but it is a corsage of flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: To accost someone and keep them talking is to detain them, and a flower worn in a lapel's slit is also called this.

clue.text: Collection of hardbacks that could be scarce at university

indicators.note: could be suggests the letters that follow might form something else if rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A set of hardback books might be hard to find in a university library.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardbacks' looks like books; it means creatures with hard shells.
explanation.definitionFit: The class of crabs, lobsters and shrimps, all armoured with hard shells, is grouped under this scientific name.

clue.text: Ceremonial cloak with jewel as finishing touch

blocks.note: a cope is a long cloak worn by clergy at ceremonies
a precious stone is a jewel

explanation.surface: A bishop's ceremonial robe is completed by adding a gem.
explanation.definitionFit: The top stone of a wall or building is laid last, so figuratively it is the culminating final flourish.

clue.text: Cross desert that's on either side

indicators.note: letters placed on either side of something surround it

blocks.note: i.e. abbreviates id est, Latin for 'that is'
to rat is to desert or betray one's side

explanation.surface: A traveller crosses a desert with sand stretching away on both sides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' and 'desert' both look like travel words; the first is the adjective meaning angry and the second a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone cross is annoyed, and irate means angry, so the adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: One sees church language initially suppressed

definitions.note: the answer is a noun naming the thing that sees

indicators.note: what is suppressed at the start is kept out, so the first letter goes

blocks.note: Coptic is the liturgical language of the Egyptian Christian church

explanation.surface: An observer notices that a church's old language is being stifled from the outset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One sees' reads as a person observing, but it is the organ of sight itself.
explanation.definitionFit: An optic is an informal or humorous name for the eye, the organ one sees with.

clue.text: Common place, say, to find parking space

blocks.note: P is the sign for a parking place
latitude is room or freedom to manoeuvre

explanation.surface: A village common is suggested as somewhere to leave a car.
explanation.walkthrough: Written as two words, 'Common place' looks like a village green; run together it is a trite remark.
explanation.definitionFit: A commonplace is a remark used so often it has lost its force, which is a platitude.

clue.text: Where to acknowledge sin arising from the lesson of Cain

indicators.note: something arising from a source is formed out of it, here by rearranging its letters

blocks.note: the twelve letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: The moral of Cain's murder of Abel teaches a sinner to own up.
explanation.definitionFit: The confessional is the booth in a Catholic church where penitents admit their sins to a priest.

clue.text: A number of musicians and others turning up in the Bible

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means the letters read from the bottom upwards
in places the turned group inside the scripture letters

blocks.note: etc. abbreviates et cetera, meaning and the rest
OT is the Old Testament

explanation.surface: Several musicians and other figures appear in scripture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A number' looks like a figure; it is a group of a set size.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of eight players or singers is an ensemble, which is a number of musicians.

clue.text: Moslem mystic starts to study unfamiliar foreign ideas

indicators.note: the starts of the next words are their opening letters

blocks.note: the first letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: A Muslim mystic begins to explore strange concepts from abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: A Sufi practises the mystical, inward tradition of Islam, so is a Muslim mystic.

clue.text: Tailless bird soaring over African mount

indicators.note: without a tail, the bird's name loses its last letter
in a down clue, soaring sends the letters upwards, so they read backwards

blocks.note: a grebe is a diving water bird

explanation.surface: A bird with no tail feathers flies high over an African mountain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mount' suggests a horse; berg is the South African word for a mountain, as in the Drakensberg.
explanation.definitionFit: In South African English, from Afrikaans, a berg is a mountain, so it is an African mount.

clue.text: Custom rejected by Biblical people

indicators.note: something rejected is turned back, so the letters are read the other way

blocks.note: mode means custom or fashion

explanation.surface: Ancient Israelites spurn a practice of their neighbours.
explanation.definitionFit: Edom was the kingdom descended from Esau in the Old Testament, so names a Biblical nation.

clue.text: Furnish criminal with testimonial

blocks.note: a con is a convict
a tribute is a statement of praise

explanation.surface: Someone supplies a convicted criminal with a character reference.
explanation.walkthrough: 'criminal' looks like an anagram signal but is a noun here.
explanation.definitionFit: To contribute is to supply or provide something, just as to furnish is to provide.

clue.text: Speak proper — is one doing a wind-up?

definitions.note: the answer is a noun; the definition describes what it does

indicators.note: speak means the next word is said out loud, not spelt

blocks.note: proper in the sense of genuine

explanation.surface: Someone is told to talk properly and suspects they are being teased.
explanation.walkthrough: A wind-up is British slang for a tease; here it is literal, as a fishing reel winds in the line.
explanation.definitionFit: A fishing reel is the spool on a rod that winds line back in, so it does winding up.

clue.text: Passing judgment, and not in mere phrases?

blocks.note: first meaning: a judge announcing the punishment after a conviction
second meaning: forming full grammatical units of speech rather than fragments

explanation.surface: A judge pronounces punishment and speaks in complete statements.
explanation.definitionFit: A court's punishment is pronounced in this act, and the word also describes building complete grammatical units.
